hypotheses: We expect an advantage for bilinguals over monolinguals if they have relatively stronger skills in the language of instruction.
Combinations of languages with similar orthographic scripts will have the highest potential compared to combinations which differ in their scripts.
claim.hypotheses_location: Page 78, Section 1.4, paragraphs exploring research questions
claim.statement: The effect of speaking a minority language at home on foreign language learning

data.source: Assessment of Reading and Mathematics Development Study (ELEMENT)
data.wave_or_subset: Data from a representative sample of students from a major European city
data.notes: Study follows a cohort of children from the fourth grade to the sixth grade

method.description: The study conducted secondary analyses of ELEMENT data to investigate bilingualism's effects on English language ability, controlling for confounding variables.
steps: Identify bilingual and monolingual students using language spoken at home.
Control for cognitive abilities and socio-economic status to measure English language achievement.
Subdivide bilinguals into language-specific groups and analyze differences.
method.models: Multiple regression analyses, controlled for background factors
method.independent_variables: Bilingual group membership, level of German proficiency
method.control_variables: Cognitive abilities, age, gender, socio-economic status, parental education, cultural capital
method.tools_software: MPlus 5.21, ConQuest for item response theory scaling

results.summary: Immigrant bilingual students generally show advantages in learning English as a foreign language. These advantages vary between specific language groups, with differences in the language of instruction being a significant factor.

numerical_results.outcome_name: English language ability advantage for bilinguals

metadata.original_paper_title: The effect of speaking a minority language at home on foreign language learning
